utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The witness was raised in and has lived all his life in Sanski Most. After the beginning of the war in Croatia in 1991, he noticed an increase in anti-Muslim propaganda on the radio and television. Checkpoints manned by the army, the military police and the regular police appeared on the roads. Initially the checkpoints were used to control people of all nationalities, but in 1992, they were used to control non-Serbs only. A Serb War Presidency, headed by Nedeljko Rasula, was established in the municipality. On about 18 April 1992, the Serb and Muslim police forces separated. Around this time, Muslims and Croats were required to return any former JNA uniforms and weapons which they had in their private possession. Muslims in the witness's village continued to patrol using hunting rifles. On 13 May 1992, the witness saw Serb families in military trucks and on tractors leaving for the mountains. On the same day, Serb forces in the village of Podlug, near Sanski Most town, used mortars and anti-aircraft cannons to fire on the village of Trnova. The following day, the witness heard that Serb forces had attacked the Muslim police in Sanski Most. Local SDS President Nedeljko Rasula later announced on the radio that all Muslims and Croats were required to hand over their remaining weapons; he said that the Serb army would guarantee peace and security. A schedule for the handover of weapons was announced. During the second half of May 1992, the freedom of movement of non-Serbs was restricted further. On the 26th of May, 1992, there was a further radio announcement that all Muslims should surrender their weapons. On the following day, regular troops and reservists gathered the population of Mahala, a predominantly Muslim part of Sanski Most town, at a soccer field. On the 28th of May, 1992, Serb artillery shelled Mahala, which was by then empty of its population. Houses in Mahala were set on fire, about four or five at a time. Refugees from Mahala began arriving at the witness's village the next day. Serb police also escorted about 700 non-Serbs to the village of Stari Majdan. On the 29th of May, 1992, the witness heard shelling and explosions at the village of Vrhpolje. On the 18th of June, 1992, Serb police arrested the witness at his house and detained him at Betonirka, a set of garages in Sanski Most town, located behind the SUP building. Betonirka is a detention facility 28.1 in Schedule C to the indictment. The witness was detained at best Betonirka for 19 days. During that period, the witness was detained in a garage which was about 5 or 6 metres long and 4 metres wide. The garage held about 30 detainees, who slept sitting down due to the lack of space. There was one window of about 60 centimetres by 30 centimetres. There were no sanitary facilities, and detainees relieved themselves in the garage. Apart from three nights, Serb reserve policemen took the witness every night of his detention to a building, where he was interrogated and beaten. Several of the witness's ribs were broken as a result. All but one of the detainees in the garage were also beaten. On the 22nd of June, 1992, the witness was taken to a location about 1 and a half kilometres from Betonirka, where over 20 men were made to dig their own graves, kneel, and were killed by having their throats cut.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Local SDS president Rasula was present at the killing site. The witness will testify today in more detail about this event, which is listed as event 17.1 in Schedule B to the indictment. "On the 7th of July, 1992, the witness and 63 other detainees were instructed to board a truck on a stiflingly hot day. Tarpaulin covered the truck. Due to the extreme heat and lack of air, a number of the detainees died on the trip to Manjaca. The witness will also testify today in greater detail about this incident, which is listed as incident 1.3 in Schedule B to the indictment. Manjaca camp is detention facility 1.4 in Schedule C to the indictment. On arrival at Manjaca, surviving detainees unloaded the dead detainees and the camp commander refused to accept a number of extremely dehydrated detainees who were about to die. The witness was detained at Manjaca in a large cattle shed for four and a half months. He will describe today the conditions of detention there, the beatings he received and saw, and the killings he witnessed. From time to time, the witness was" -- excuse me. "From the time the witness was arrested in June until his release in November, his weight reduced from 90 kilogrammes to 55 kilogrammes." This witness's testimony is relevant to all counts in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you a few questions about your evidence. I'd like to concentrate, first of all, on the period after the police force split into a Serb force and a non-Serb force. You said in paragraph 11 of your statement that the SOS, the White Eagles, and the local SUP of Sanski Most worked together on a regular basis. What was it that made you believe that they worked together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: In simple terms, all those wearing uniforms, that is, the JNA uniforms, the SOS uniforms, which were at that time not called the Army of Republika Srpska. Their commander was Dusko Saovic, also known as Njunja. In my view, he was the commander because he had a white headband, he had long hair, and he was the one who was leading them. They all had access to town, and they carried weapons in town. They could walk normally. Before that, I would like to say something else. The JNA had blocked the town and the police station even before that, and it was only then, even before the attack on the police station, while people were still moving freely, you could see Chetniks moving around, JNA troops and other units while it was still all right for them to move around. I believe that it was on the 27th or the 28th of May. So one could see that they were moving about freely, whereas us civilians, Muslims and Croats, we were all stopped at checkpoints, whereas they were never stopped and checked. They could go through the checkpoints without any hindrance and they carried arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You referred to checkpoints where you were stopped and controlled but Serbs with not stopped and controls. Which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. forces were manning those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Up to the moment when the police were divided, it was the JNA and there were some Muslims with them up to April -- actually, up to Bajram, and I can't tell you when Bajram was in the year 1992. As from then on, all the Muslims and Croats were removed, and from then on the soldiers in olive-drab uniforms were there. There was the army. There were rifles, and the police were in containers. This was the checkpoint at the crossroads, as I was going from my village to the town. There is a crossroads there that is in the shape of a cross, and it is on the right-hand side as you start walking from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, could you -- in your statement, you mentioned the presence of White Eagles, Seselj's men, in the municipality. Did you see -- as well as the SOS. Did you see the White Eagles and Seselj's men working with police at the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that question. Of course, the statement is in evidence. I think it's preferable if questions are to be asked to the witness, that they not be asked in a leading fashion in relation to specific areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, if no question is asked about it, then of course the statement is in evidence, so if it would add something to what is in the statement, I would agree with you; if it's, as we see happen now and then, if it's mainly seeking confirmation of what is in the statement as a -- well, as a start for further questions, then I would not mind if the witness is led. Would you please keep that in mind, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you said that Nedeljko Rasula, the local SDS president, and president of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff, was your teacher in elementary school and in secondary school. How often did you see Mr. Rasula in the period leading up to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, may I ask you something: Don't you seek any confirmation any more from what you just asked the witness? Or do you think it is something you should ask in a different way? Because we have not received any answer before we heard the -- well, "objection" is perhaps true strong a word, but the suggestion by Ms. Loukas not to lead the witness. You asked him about --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- about -- at least, working together, were there any groups who were working together. Yes. Would you please revisit that point, because we might be in a --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, at the checkpoints, who, if anyone, did the Serb police work together with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: At that checkpoint that I had to pass on my way home from work, there were no Seselj Chetniks or White Eagles, but they were at the checkpoint towards the Stari Majdan, on the Sanski Most-Prijedor road. There was a checkpoint there at the crossroads; one road led to Prijedor, and that's where they were manning the checkpoint. They were stationed some 500 metres away in a little wood under the tents. When I say "they," I'm referring to Seselj's men and to the White Eagles. On several occasions while I still worked, I went to Majdan, to Gumera [phoen]. There is a rubber factory there that is used for axles on vehicles, and that's how I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one additional question: You said where the Seselj and the White Eagles people were manning checkpoints. Do I properly understand your testimony that on those checkpoints there were just the Seselj's men and the White Eagles? No other groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the checkpoint on the Majdan-Prijedor road, they were the ones that were manning that point, whereas the checkpoint on the road from my village to town, they were not there. They would come every now and then, but they wouldn't check people. They did check me once, but they did not ill-treat me. They inspected my official documents and they let me go. In Sanski Most, however, they did not check people, but in Majdan, at that crossroads, they were the ones who controlled that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And they were the exclusive present people at that checkpoint at the Majdan-Prijedor road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there others then as well, and who were they, at that specific checkpoint, Majdan-Prijedor road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were stationed there, some 500 metres away towards Majdan, you know, and they probably controlled those who were passing because of their camp that was situated a little bit further away. They did not do anything to me. They did check me. Some of them had the insignia kokarda on their caps and the others had white banding on their armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please listen carefully to my question. My question was whether at that checkpoint where you said the Seselj and the White Eagles were, the Seselj men, were there any -- at that checkpoint any other groups? Whatever groups. Or were there just the Seselj and the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was passing by, they were there alone. There was five of them when I was passing through. Maybe there were some later on; however, I didn't see that, and I can't tell you what I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you about Mr. Rasula, who was your teacher in elementary and high school. Did you see Mr. Rasula at all in early 1992 before June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him. Sometime after New Year, he came to the mine, and he had a word with my bosses. I was present there. I wasn't there all the time. I stayed with them for some ten minutes or so. I attended that technical meeting. After that, I had to tend to my duties. I don't know what they were talking about. And I also saw him once in June, when I went to collect my paycheck. The war had already started. I saw him in the restaurant. That was around noon. I saw him and the others from the Crisis Staff. They were sitting in the Slozna Braca restaurant, because my administrative building was across the road from that restaurant, so one could see them sitting in that restaurant. You could see them as you were leaving the building because the tables were in front of the restaurant, and I found it a bit odd to know that houses were being set on fire in the town and at the same time the president of the Municipality and the president of the Crisis Staff were sitting in a restaurant. I found that very odd at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In which garage, looking at it from left to right, were you detained? Just indicate to the Judges as best you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: In the last, in the third, as you are looking from the right to the left. Or the first one, if you're looking from the left to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's the closest garage to the camera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: No. No. It is actually the furthest, and the door of that garage is closed. Because the photo was taken from the back. Here you can see the gate, the gate leading to the garages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I would request that the witness be shown the next exhibit, which is also a photograph. And I'd request that that be given the next number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be P218. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this photograph -- this building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes. This is the garage where I was detained. You can see the window on the right-hand side here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, was that window open while you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: The window was open, but there was a pallet full of bricks very high up, so even if -- when the window was open, nobody could escape through the window, because there were bricks placed one on top of the other in front of the window. So nobody could get out through the window, even if it was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And isn't it right that during the 19 days of your detention there were about 30 of you at any given time in that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes. There were some 30 of us. Only on Tuesdays there were fewer of us because on Tuesdays people were transported, so on Tuesday there would be about 15 of us and on Wednesdays new detainees would be brought in and placed in the garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How many hours a day were you kept in that garage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: What do you mean how many hours? The only time I didn't spend in the garage was when I was taken to be beaten, and that was the only time I didn't spend in the garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And what was the temperature like in that garage while you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: We didn't know that, but it was terribly hot. The garage did not have a roof but just a concrete slate. There was no protection against the heat. This concrete slate even increased the temperature. And when the day was sunny, anybody who found themselves in the garage was suffering. There were people who would faint during the day. We did not receive enough water. We would only receive maybe two, three, or four decilitres of water during the day, and that was all the water we had, the drinking water, the water to dress our wounds after we were beaten. That was all the water that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the air like in the garage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: The air in the garage was terrible. We were all stinking from the excrement that was there that couldn't be cleaned away, so that it was really unbearable. But there you are. I survived. If there were 30 of us in the garage - and it was about 6 by 4 metres in size, which makes it 24 square metres - let us say that there was about 70 cubic metres of air. And oxygen accounts for 21 per cent. One needs 3 and a half cubic metres of air to be able to breathe normally. And there must be some flow of air, because the doors didn't fit absolutely, so that is what helped us survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it right, sir, that while you were working in the mine, that you were a member of a mine rescue team and so you have some amount of experience in the amount of air required by a human being to survive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that, again, I don't -- if there is going to be additional information to the statement, I think it's appropriate that it's not led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question to you was -- and I'll reformulate it -- what gave you specific knowledge on how much air a human being would need to live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In every mine that has underground pits, a team of rescue workers is formed should methane explode or coal dust, and these people had to be fit physically and mentally to extend first aid to the injured on the spot, so I went through special training for three months for extending first aid in the case of such accidents. The doctor who trained us gave us instructions as to the quantity of oxygen a human being needs. We had special equipment, isolation equipment. Should we notice there was a shortage of oxygen, then we would have a special meter to show us how much air we could give to the injured person through our own equipment to help that person overcome the problem. So if the doctor told me wrong, I am telling you wrong as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I instruct you as follows: The question was: What gave you special knowledge? You told us in quite some detail on what exactly the doctor told you, but if you would have first answered that you got special training as a mine rescue worker including knowledge on the air one needs to survive, that would have been sufficient at this moment, even without going into so many details, because we're under some time restrictions and the main reason for putting this question to you is to find out what gave you this special knowledge, rather than on how you gained it specifically, but where did you get it -- at that course, given by a doctor. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said that on the third day of your detention - this is paragraph 35, Your Honours - you were taken to the SUP station for interrogation. Who took you to the SUP station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: A reserve policeman wearing a police uniform, Kravic. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What were you interrogated about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Well, they asked about weapons, why I hadn't handed over my weapons, whether I had any weapons, and they said I did have weapons. Actually, they were right, only I told them that I didn't at first. I didn't want to admit that I had a weapon, but I did. And I said this in my statement. Because if I had admitted to having the weapon, I certainly wouldn't be here today. All those who admitted were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: All those who had weapons and surrendered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement - again, at paragraph 36, Your Honours - you said that after the interrogation finished, a reserve policeman called Kravic took you out of the office and Dusko Zoric told him to push you down the stairway. The policeman hit you with a rifle on the back and you fell down the stairs. You landed on the first landing, and the policeman kicked you in the back again. You fell down the stairs again and you had to stand up immediately to avoid more beating. You say that you were in substantial pain and discomfort and you still have a scar from the rifle butt. I have two questions about that: First, did you receive any medical attention from this injury?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: No. No. There weren't any doctors there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Second, is there any continuing pain and discomfort to you as a result of that injury?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes, I suffer. But it's -- I was beaten up. In the back I have a scar from the rifle butt which tore off a piece of tissue, and it's quite visible on my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, you said that you were beaten on all but three nights that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you were in Betonirka. Now, apart from the SUP building where you were beaten on the third night, where were you beaten on all the other nights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Next to the Betonirka there is what is known as the administrative building. It leans on the Betonirka, and there are three premises there, and then in the evening around 10.00 they would start to beat us. They would take us from the garage, beat us up. They would say that they started work at about 10.00 when it fell dark, as it was summertime, and they would beat people so badly. They did all kinds of things. They cursed. They never asked me the same questions when they took me for this what they called interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said that they would typically start beating you at 10.00. How long approximately were you beaten for on an average night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Well, it depended, how many people would join them from the outside. Even young people, children, even people who were my subordinates would come, if they left work early, and I had to take down these things. If they were supposed to work for eight hours a day, I would write that down, and then he would come and take his revenge on me, and all kinds of things happened there, not just to me but to everyone. If a man would fall down -- but if I were to go into these details, I would need to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, you said that people would join "them" from the outside. When you used the word "them," who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: The policemen, the guards who were guarding us in the Betonirka, because five or six of them normally couldn't guard them -- guard 90 of us. Then they would call in young men from the coffee bars. People who knew we were there would beat us. I can explain in greater detail the things that were happening, but I wouldn't like that to be done in public. These are things that a normal person would never do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, during those beatings, did you normally remain conscious, or did you normally lose consciousness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Sometimes I would lose consciousness, and on other occasions I would remain conscious. And then if that other person would faint, then we would have to pick him up and take him back running. For example, should he have a bowel movement in an unconscious state - and as I said, there were three rooms and they were beating in three groups - so we would have to carry this person out quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, could you confirm with a yes or no: Were you always forced to remain seated, or were you sometimes forced to stand upright?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Sometimes after the beating we were forced to stand up, upright, with our heads bent and our arms on our back, and we would stand like that until we would fall down. And then if somebody fell down, we would pick him up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I propose now to move you to the 22nd of June, 1992. In statement, you describe an incident at Kriva Cesta. Now, sir, you said you were taken out of a garage in the morning and put you in a car. That car went to Kriva Cesta. When you arrived there and you got out of the car, where exactly did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: When I arrived, they shoved me out of the car, opened the boot, and told me to pick up a shovel. The road was above the stream. There was a 5- or 6-metre embankment, and they told know go down to the stream.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, when you are using the word "they" -- you say "they shoved me out of the car." Who was "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: The policemen. And in my statement, you have the names. You must understand, I mustn't mention the names, because if I do that -- shall we go into private session and then I can give you the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, sir. Thank you. It's in your statement, and the Judges have your statement. We'll remain in open session. Sir, you said that they told you to go down to the stream. Now, on your arrival at the stream, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: They told me to dig. I looked around, and I saw men standing on my right, and there were another two who came to stand on my left, and I saw that they all had shovels in their hands, and we were told to dig. I knew what I was digging. No one needed to explain anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How long did you dig for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I don't know. It was difficult to dig because as you dug a hole, the water would take away the earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What did you do when you had finished digging the hole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I stood looking as much as I dared to and as much as it was possible to see at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: As there were willows there, I saw men in uniform standing with their rifles pointed at us, and a little further away, some 50 metres, I saw Nedeljko Rasula and some other men whose names are given in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Why are you -- what was Rasula doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: He was sitting. They were about 50 metres away and they were sitting at a table.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What were they doing at the table?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Eating and drinking, at least as far as I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said that you and some others were forced to dig. Approximately how many others were forced to dig?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: In my judgement, there were about 20, 22, 23 men to my right, as far as I was able to judge. There weren't two or three, but in my estimate that many. One of those was found.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What did you hear around this time, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: First I heard gurgling, screaming, and I thought that my turn had come. A few pistol shots could be heard, and the man next to me - and I said this in my statement - I recognised him as he fell. He turned around with his face towards me, and I could see from his neck that blood was coming from the left side of his neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the cause of that blood coming from the left side of his neck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: As I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you have preferred to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to explain at this very moment. We'll first turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's confirmed on my screen that we are now in open session again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'm now going to ask you some questions. We're back in open session. If at any point you want to return to private session, please just say so. I'd like to take you to the last day of your detention at Betonirka, which was the 7th of July, 1992. Now, you mentioned that a number of you were beaten on the morning of the 7th of July. Were you personally beaten on the morning of the 7th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes, I was personally beaten on that day. The man that I remember very well who beat me, he had a piece of wood with knobs 1 centimetre apart. I was doing exercises, and he was beating me and he was also -- there were two others that were standing on -- to my side, and they were kicking me with their feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you lose consciousness or did you retain consciousness after that beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I was neither conscious or -- nor did I faint. I would faint and then I would come to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to the moment that you were loaded onto a truck. How many of you were loaded onto that truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time how many of us were loaded onto that truck. I didn't know the number until we arrived in Manjaca. In Manjaca I learnt that there were 64 of us. One of the inspectors who was escorting the convoy told us that there were 64 of us from Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: After the truck left Betonirka, did it go directly to Manjaca without stopping? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: No. No, it didn't. It stopped. The truck had a canvas cover, and that canvas cover could be locked. For example, nowadays when you have a truck crossing the border, it can be sealed. Instead of that seal that trucks have today, this truck had a lock. It was locked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How much fresh air was there in that truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: It was scorchingly hot on that day. Under the canvas cover, it was hard to breathe. The canvas could not be opened; it was locked, as I've said. When the truck stopped for the second time to be checked, according to what we heard - this was on the Vrhpolje bridge - by then, one lad started dying. I believe that his name can be found in the statement. On that day, it was his eighteenth birthday. He was the first one to die in that truck. And then people started dying one after another, because there was no air in the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How much water did you have in the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: There was no water at all, none whatsoever. I had a little flask, an aftershave flask with water. I drank that, and then I used the flask to urinate in, and then I drank urine. I found a rotten apple in the truck. That's what I had to eat. And I believe that this is how I survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the distance between Betonirka and Manjaca is not an extremely long distance. Could you explain to the Judges why it took so long for the journey from Betonirka to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Well, in my view, this was done just to torture us. It seemed like an eternity to me. We arrived in Manjaca at dusk, and we left Betonirka around 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning. It was summertime, and it was dusk, so I reckon it must have been sometime around 9.00 or half past 9.00 in the evening, and we departed around 11.00 in the morning. I did not have a watch, because when I arrived at Betonirka everything was taken away from us -- money, personal documents, watches, jewellery -- so we couldn't actually tell the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said that on the truck there was no water at all. Did you ask the guards for water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: At one place when we stopped, we did ask for water. We were shouting, "Water. Water." And some women wanted to give us water, but they chased them away. I don't know who the women were. We couldn't see that. I only know that we were shouting to be given some water.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you ask the guards to let in more fresh air?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: We didn't have an occasion to do that. We tried to take our clothes off, and then we wanted to wedge our shoes between the canvas cover and the lorry sides. When we did that, they would snatch those away. They would fire shots in the air. They would curse our mothers and insult us, and they would say, "Look at them. They want air."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you just clarify that when you used the word "they would snatch our shoes away and they would fire shots in the air," who are you referring to when you used the word "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: The policemen who were our escorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, on your arrival at Manjaca, when the truck stopped, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Well, when the truck stopped when we arrived at Manjaca, they opened the canvas cover, and when they did that, literally they told us, "See how they stink, the balijas. Fuck their mothers," when they opened the canvas cover in the back. And then they told us to get out. First they started calling our names, but those who had died did not respond, and then they told us that those of us who had survived should get off the truck. And when we got off, a man introduced himself to us. He gave us his nickname. He introduced himself as Fadil Bula. We were told to pull out those who still gave some signs of life. We were told to pull them off the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you remember how many of the detainees were dead when you arrived at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: As I was sitting next to the driver's cabin, I was the last to get off the truck. According to my estimate, there were maybe 19 -- 18 or 19 people who had died. It was very difficult to count. However, I could see that some had died sitting down. The person that I mentioned before died in my lap. It was very difficult to get off the truck. You had to step over the dead bodies. I believe that they took off some six people who were still alive, but just barely. Then the camp commander came and said, "This Muslim shit is not entering the camp alive." Before that, Dr. Sabanovic came, and when he examined them, he was a detainee himself. He said that they needed some medical assistance because they were dehydrated. The commander said, "There's no such thing." And then he said, "The shit has to go back onto the truck because I don't need them in the camp."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to focus on those six detainees who you said were still alive but just barely. Did you ever see any of those six men again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them. The 19 that I was referring to were found in 1992 or in 1993. Their bodies were buried, and the DNA analysis was used to establish the identity of five of them. And as for the others, I never saw them again and they're still missing and their bodies are still being looked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I'd like to show the next exhibit, which is a video. I'd request that this be given an exhibit number. The B/C/S and English transcripts of this video are available. The content of the transcripts, for Your Honours's guidance, is not enormously valuable. It's the images that are of importance in this video. This video is made up of a number of clips from CNN, BBC, and Sky News. They have B/C/S subtitles, and we have added English subtitles, which will appear at the very bottom of your screen underneath the B/C/S subtitles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First a number will be attributed to the video.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the CD gets the exhibit number P219, the English transcript gets the exhibit number P219.A; and the B/C/S transcript gets the exhibit number P219.A.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just check whether we always put a dot between the number and the letter, but the 219A at least. Yes. Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Just in relation to this question of the video. Obviously the purpose for which the Prosecution seeks to tender the video was on the basis of the visual images. And as I understand it from what Mr. Gaynor has just said, there's no reliance placed on the transcript. Now, in those circumstances, Your Honour, I would be objecting to the transcript coming in as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not consent. The transcripts in question - you'll see the video in a moment - you have a little bit of the normal news presentation commentary that ordinarily accompanies videos of this kind from CNN, BBC, and Sky News. They're of assistance simply in understanding what you're looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please review those parts of the transcript, Mr. Gaynor, that are really serving that. For example, I'm just reading very quickly. If you say what we saw was a shed and in the better days might have housed animals. Now it homes more than 600 men," that's a kind of description of Manjaca. That clearly indicates what we see. On the other hand, if we hear a male voice saying: "The prisoners told us how it was even more tragic in the Omarska camp," then of course that has got nothing to do with what we see but just gives additional information. So perhaps you could review what is adding to the pictures and what is just -- because then we introduce a lot of hearsay opinion, which as such is not inadmissible, but -- and, of course, if we say "The conditions are detained -- are not even for animals, let alone people," as you may be aware, there's quite a lot of discussion on what should be granted to animals, so therefore even the threshold would be -- but I do Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. understand. So it's a lot of additional impressions and additional opinion that is contained in it. So if you would please, then, identify what in your view is most relevant in the transcript. And if you, please, could tell us what you think is essential. What do we need in addition to what we see? I do understand it's about Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've just conferred with Mr. Tieger. In our view, the nature of this evidence is really no different to a newspaper article or written forms of media evidence which we tender and are accepted in evidence as a matter of course. Now, it may be that Your Honours might wish to see the video, review the transcript, and decide that perhaps it should be admitted in evidence. If you'd prefer for us to select those parts that we do want to have in evidence, we can do so after this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, a decision has still to be taken on admission. And as is the case in -- let's say in Bench trials, usually you have the material in front of you before you decide whether or not to admit it in full or not. So let's play the video, but please be aware that not everything of the transcript might be such that the Chamber could accept it as a basis for forming its opinion in this case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video is, I think, a little bit under four minutes long. I think the best way is simply to play the video in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: REPORTER 1: Paddy Ashdown had broken his holiday and travelled for three days over a thousand miles to get to Manjaca camp. What he saw was a shed that in better days might have housed animals. Now it homes more than 600 men. Here the prisoners eat, sleep and live 24 hours a day. Most of these men just arrived three days ago from the camp at Omarska. Their faces still haunted by memories they did not dare relate in the presence of their guards. For five minutes Paddy Ashdown was allowed to speak privately to the men. However grim their conditions here, they told him, things are much better than the place they had just come from. The camp commandant had promised Mr. Ashdown total freedom to see anything he wanted. In the event, he was told that wasn't possible. Even during Mr. Ashdown's visit, time was limited to a mere half hour and access was limited to only a few prisoners. As he left, he said that however bleak things seemed to be, this camp could appear to be properly run. PADDY ASHDOWN: Clearly I had access to those prisoners without the guards' presence. I detest their conditions and I find them disbelievable. They've had an appalling time in Omarska, where they'd come from. I think it's a tremendous achievement on the part of the press to have exposed that and based on that they've saved very many people's lives. But every prisoner I spoke to here, without the guards' presence, has told me that, "Conditions are not what we want them to be but they're a hell of a lot better than what they were before." REPORTER 1: With the visiting politicians gone, what these men have suffered in the past remains largely unspoken. Caroline Hurt in the Manjaca Prison Camp in Bosnia. REPORTER 2: Manjaca is a military camp in Serbian-held Northern Bosnia. Authorities say they hold 3.500 prisoners here, including about 1.000 from the notorious Omarska camp. Pictures of emaciated captives in detention centres last week outraged the international community and prompted the Serbian leaders to quickly transfer a hundred into this military facility. This terrified little prisoner mumbles that conditions here are slightly better. "We get enough food now," says this man. We were only allowed to interview two inmates, and in each case the soldiers immediately wanted to know what we had asked. This is one of the camps officials from the International Red Cross say they will be inspecting this week. Indeed, the president of Bosnia's Serbs has offered to hand them control of all of these detention centres. The Serb leadership is under tremendous pressure to allow outsiders access to these camps. The proposed UN resolution would authorise any means necessary to implement that access, as well as guarantee the supply of humanitarian aid. Still, even though Karadzic himself authorised our visit to this camp, journalists were allowed less than half an hour to assess the situation. Soldiers moved us along rapidly, allowing us to take very few pictures and to ask even fewer questions. The camp commandant insists that the Geneva Conventions are being respected, but those prisoners we asked maintained they are civilians, not soldiers. Those we saw are crammed into cattle sheds where they spend all day and all night, huddled together like animals. They are permitted to leave these quarters only briefly to a small ration of bread and soup. Christiane Amanpour, CNN, Manjaca in Northern Bosnia.

utterances.text: Yes. May I first ask you, Mr. Gaynor, before we continue, is this a literal translation? utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as far as times are concerned, even knowledge of the B/C/S language would not help you, is it? utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could just indicate for the benefit of the Trial Chamber that Ms. Cmeric, who of course is a B/C/S speaker, has indicated to me that so far going through the document there seems to be -- perhaps a problem with the actual times that are indicated in the document and not so much with the content, apart from a certain area where there seems to be -- I think which Your Honour also identified was in relation to -- yeah, just a sentence at one point that seems to be not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. dealt with in the other version. But at this point, that's what Ms. Cmeric has pointed out to me, for the benefit of the Court. There seems to be some issue in relation to the actual times that are placed on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Obviously that needs to be clarified, but I thought I'd bring this up at this point --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the image on the screen in front of you -- Mr. 565, do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: What is that building?

utterances.text: It's the camp that used to be a cow shed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to come closer to the microphone. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the detention camp. Before that, I think it was a cow shed, because we could see where the cattle were eating and sleeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is that the building in which you were detained at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in that video, you might have seen a British politician, Mr. Ashdown, suggesting that the catch was well run. And I'd like to ask you a few questions about that. How much were you given to eat on a typical day during your detention at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I can explain what the food was like. They would take a loaf of bread of 800 grams. Then they would cut it in two, then again lengthwise, so you'd get four quarters of one loaf. So one loaf of 800 grams. It was brown bread. And then it would be cut up into 44 parts. If there was tea in the morning, it was tea without sugar. And if it was beans, you'd get ten beans in a plate, because that was all. Or if it was cabbage, then you'd get two leaves of cabbage. The rest was just water that wasn't salty or had no gravy or anything in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How much did you receive to drink at Manjaca on a typical day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: On their -- in their military rubber pots, they would bring about 30 litres for us, and there would be 800 of us, and this would be distributed in such a way that a person would get half a glass of water. Sometimes the first one to drink would take a little more than half. Then the other one would have less left. Anyway, it wasn't sufficient. And water was distributed twice; on rare occasions, three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How often did you wash yourself at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Not at all. Only when the International Red Cross came, they assembled a kind of military showers outside, and they allowed a couple of detainees to shower while they were there, and while the television was filming, they were bathing. And after that, we were not allowed to bathe. And it was only when the Red Cross installed themselves there permanently that they brought us plastic jerrycans with which we went to fetch water, and then we could wash ourselves, but this started towards the end of August. But up until then no one had a proper bath, nor could they wash their teeth. There was lice. And that's how it was. Some people got diarrhoea because of the very poor hygiene.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, you referred to the -- that you got a very small piece of bread. They would take a loaf of 800 grams and cut it up into 44 parts. How often per day did you receive a piece of bread of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Twice. And when they said they didn't have any, we would get it only once, but mostly we got it twice a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, you must have been extremely hungry. Did you try to get food from anywhere outside the barn?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I didn't try to get any food until the International Red Cross came. And as I was saying, that didn't happen until the end of August. And once when I went to the toilet, I'd pick some grass and started eating it, and then I got slapped and cursed at. The grass was best around the toilet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, may I ask you one thing: Is there any dispute about food being far below what a human being needs, water to be far below what a human being needs, sanitary conditions very bad in Manjaca? Is that something in dispute; yes or no? It's --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not an area I intend to cross-examine on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the witness statement and -- of course, this could have been discussed between the parties. I do understand that the conditions in Manjaca camp were such that provision of food was totally insufficient, provision of water was totally insufficient, sanitary conditions were totally insufficient, and I would have to look at the indictment to see exactly what was still -- medical care, I think, was similar, I take it, Ms. Loukas, insufficient. I have to check in the indictment what exactly Mr. Krajisnik has been charged with in this respect as far as the conditions of Manjaca camp are concerned, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can just indicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: Further in relation to the question that Your Honours asked me, is that I don't propose to cross-examine in relation to the conditions at Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And it's certainly not an area that I could have instructions from my client on. He, of course, did not know what was happening at Manjaca camp, and it's not an area I'd propose to cross-examine on.

utterances.text: He might have found out later. That's a possibility. He could have instructed you. But I do understand that you have received no instructions in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least what I do understand is that they accept the evidence. They do not dispute the correctness of the evidence as such. Is that a correct understanding, Ms. Loukas? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as I've indicated, it's not an area in which my client can give instructions, so it's not an area, of course, that I propose to cross-examine this witness on, or to, in terms of, you know, Rule 90(H) under the Rules of this Tribunal, or more formally known as Browne and Dunn under Anglo system, I am not in a position to cross-examine in relation to those issues and I don't propose to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do then understand, because I think then that is the issue, that your client couldn't instruct you because he has no personal knowledge of it. utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, especially since we're working on the -- also on the basis of a written statement, I'd like you to limit yourself to those parts that really add something to what's already on paper. utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, you were inspected by the Red Cross, and I'd like you to tell the Court -- that was in about mid-July. I'd like you to tell the Court what happened to you on the night after you were inspected by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I allowed them to examine me. The lady was from Geneva. After that, they came to fetch me and said that I would go to the clinic. Actually, they didn't take me to the clinic, but they beat me up in front of the building, just in front of this shed. They took me round the corner and they beat me. They beat me up badly. I would lose consciousness and come back to, and that -- I think they thought I was already dead, and they said that they would go and beat the others who had allowed the International Red Cross to examine them, so that that is what happened to me. And in that condition, I heard cries and screams and I saw people taken to be beaten. The next day in the morning I had to get up because there was no possibility of remaining lying down, because I would be beaten again. And when I went for breakfast, I saw them carrying out two dead people. The names of those people I do not wish to mention, because they're in the statement. Actually, they beat three men that night, but two of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. In your previous answer, could you explain to the Court who you mean when you used the word "they."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: The people that they mentioned, the names they said of the men that they were going to beat because they had let themselves be examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Who beat you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Bula, Bulatovic, Zoka, and a third man whom I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And who were they? What position did they hold at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I said at the beginning that when we arrived -- he said that he was a Muslim, and he said -- he cursed at us, "Why aren't you in the proper army? You see, you're prisoners of war now." So I assume that he was one of the commanders in the camp, but in any event, he wore a military police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember an incident where guards discovered a detainee who was hiding a small candle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. Actually, he wasn't hiding this candle. These people came from the sports hall, about 800 of them, on the same day that we had come, and in that sports hall they had candles. All the prisoners from my town had candles, as they were separating the men from the women, and when they were being searched, they found this small piece of candle on him. They beat him so badly that the door -- a sliding door would open up, and they continued beating him until he fainted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.text: Now, Witness, obviously that -- the statement that's now in evidence before the Court is a statement that you gave over some three days. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.text: One date and what I just said in paragraph 68. There's just one sentence which is not correct. It is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, of course, I think you understand, Witness, that there is a very important role, in terms of the Defence, to ask questions and for you to answer truthfully, and the -- there is, I think -- if I might put it this way, not a great deal of use in attempting to second-guess what I might be asking. utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, when you were taken out of Betonirka garage, it would be true to say, would it not, that you were obviously very scared when you left the garage?

utterances.text: And when you arrived at that particular -- at your destination - I don't want to mention any names lest we identify you - but when you arrived at the destination, it would be true to say that you were, I would imagine, even more frightened when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565

utterances.text: I could not have been under more stress than I was when I first arrived there. I don't know what you're referring to when you say "enormous stress." I was under stress. utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
