utterances.text: Please go do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you'll see, Witness, that I asked you this question -- Remember, we've been through the situation of great stress, the limited time period, a matter of seconds, and the distance. Now, what I'm -- what I'm suggesting is that being absolutely fair, it's possible that it wasn't Mr. Rasula sitting at that picnic table. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: First of all, I know Rasula's voice. Second of all, that morning, when I was being put in the Mercedes, Rasula was driving ahead of us. And what I saw on him -- the clothes, the chequered coat, a shirt, and a red tie. And especially his voice when he said to them to leave me alone. And I could not have been mistaken, because the clothes that he wore were very typical of him and his clothes. And his handwriting I can recognise any day.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, of course, if you look in the statement that you have before you where you discuss this particular incident, you don't mention that Rasula was driving ahead of us. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I do, and I didn't. He did take off in his car. At that moment, I did not know what his direction was when they were putting me in the car. I know where Rasula lives. I know where his apartment is. And he went this way and then that way, and the facility where I was was on that road and the one that we saw in the photo, and there's just a sliding door through which you could see that. He never asked me. Nobody ever asked me whether I had seen Rasula at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: At which moment, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is working or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think everything works. If you are -- the question was: You said, "Nobody ever asked me whether I had seen Rasula at that moment." The question was: At what moment you meant to refer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that morning. Nobody asked me whether I saw Rasula that morning. None of the investigators asked me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the situation is, I think, you're indicating that -- you're now indicating that you saw Rasula earlier that morning and that your recognition comes in the form of the clothes that were being worn. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct. I saw him as he was passing in his car. Because he stopped for a moment. It was his younger son who was driving the car, and he was in the passenger seat, and he was to the left from the facility where I was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, so, Witness, in relation to that question I asked you whether or not you'd be prepared to concede that you're possibly mistaken about Mr. Rasula being there, you tell the Court that you're not prepared to concede that possibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: It is correct. How am I going to deny what I saw? It would be as if I did not see this pencil that is in front of me. I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in response to that -- the suggestion I made that it's possible you're mistaken, you go on to indicate, having seen Rasula earlier, a matter that's not contained in your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness said that already, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm finishing off on this point. These are the final questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas asked you whether it's true that you did not mention that you saw Rasula earlier that morning to -- during the interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, she did ask me that, and I said that the investigator had not asked me that. And since nobody asked me, I didn't say anything. I just answered the investigator's questions, and that was my role. I just answered what I knew. And if nobody asked me, I didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you blame the investigators for not asking you the right questions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, this is an inadmissible question. That's not what the witness suggests. He just says, "I answered questions," and he's not blaming anyone, but he's mainly telling us how it went. Therefore, I think the suggestion is incorrect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. So basically what you're stating to the Court is if somebody doesn't ask you about something in the context of a three-day record of interview and opportunities for corrections, you don't do anything other than specifically the question asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we must object. This is paraphrasing something which the witness has clearly not said. Secondly, we're not entirely sure why it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is what the witness said, because the witness said, "I didn't give any -- if something was not asked to me, I would not have told anything about it." I'll take over for just one second. Did you during this interview ever come up with something you had in your mind as being important or relevant and included this in your statement, although not specifically asked about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did that very rarely, you know, because if a statement is very big, then it is not concise. And I just answered questions. This is what I did. Because if, for example, a question is not put to me to the effect, "Did you see Rasula on that morning," I -- how could I answer something that was never asked of me? How am I going to blame the Prosecution for not putting questions to me? They did put questions to me, and whatever questions they put to me, I answered within the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said you rarely came up with something they did not specifically ask you. Do you remember an example of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me add something about the questions not being put to me. This happened very rarely. It did happen that I added something, but there were also some questions that were not thoroughly answered to. There were some things that I meant to say, but I did not say it to the end. Sometimes I didn't give all the details, because I also wrote a diary, and even my diary does not contain all the details of the events for various reasons, because this was not done either for the public or for the press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked you whether you remembered an example of something you came up with without being asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't tell them anything that they didn't ask me. I tried to be as precise in my answers as possible. Do you understand? They put questions to me, and I would make sure that I answered exactly what happened, whether something had happened or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. You said, "It happened rarely." That's why I asked you whether you still had an example of such a rare occasion in your memory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to the investigators or are you referring to the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the interviews with the investigators.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very rarely did I volunteer information. It didn't happen -- it didn't happen that I would tell them things they didn't ask me about. The only thing I told them, and I volunteered, was that I had a weapon. I didn't want to lie to them, because somebody might have testified here that I had a weapon, and if I hadn't told them -- told that to the investigator, obviously I have would have lied to them. I didn't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas. And perhaps for your guidance, the importance of leaving this out seems not to be overwhelming, the part you asked questions about.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The importance of leaving out the ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not coming up with it by the witness himself, that he -- there was an earlier occasion when he -- I mean, that's the whole issue. You're asking about -- well, we're talking about how important it was that he did not mention that. He told us that he was not asked about this. Now, we could add another ten questions, but it's of course the judgement of how -- whether one would expect someone to come up with that spontaneously rather than being asked, and that's, of course, a matter on which the witness could only to a limited extent assist us in basing our judgement upon. Do you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's not clear enough, I'll ask the witness to take his headphone off. Could you take off your headphones for one second. Yes. The whole issue is he didn't tell it to the investigators, at least it has not been written down. How important is this aspect as to expect someone to come up with spontaneously, if not specifically asked about? I mean, that's the issue. It's not specifically a matter of fact. It's rather a question of judgement on how reliable-unreliable is a witness who doesn't come up with this detail, and that's something even asking five, six, seven more questions to that -- on that issue to the witness will not really add substantially to forming a judgement on whether one could expect, then, whether -- how -- and the reliability of the witness in this respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that, Your Honour. That's -- I understand Your Honour's point. I will just ask two more questions on this topic, if I may, and then I will leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But keep it as close to the facts as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I just want to ask you this question: Surely you've been in a situation where you thought you saw someone you knew from afar and realised when you got up close that you were wrong. Surely you've had that situation happen to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes. It does happen sometimes. Everybody has experienced that. It's only human.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And, of course, I take it when you were in conference with the Prosecution yesterday, they discussed with you this question of the identification of Mr. Rasula?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you didn't think to tell them yesterday about this additional piece of identifying evidence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Let's be clear on one thing: This is not an additional piece of identifying evidence. I know this person's voice very well, and he was my elementary school teacher for four years. In January 1992, we were sitting at the same table. So if none of the things had occurred prior to my seeing him, I would have still recognised his voice. If none of the things that never occurred to me to tell them, I would still recognise this man by the voice. Don't forget the fact that I worked under the ground for 30 years and I was really very good at recognising people's voices in the dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just looking at your paragraph, paragraph 47 of your statement. Could you have a look at that, Witness. Do you have that paragraph before you, Witness 565?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you'll recall that you told the Court today that you heard Rasula's voice. Do you recall giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, of course, in that paragraph, you don't say anything about hearing Rasula's voice; do you concede that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: It is not mentioned here. That's correct. However, it can be found in my diary. I wrote my diary in 1992, and this fact is mentioned there. Find my diary, look at my diary, and I'm sure you'll find it there. Here, you are right, it doesn't say that, but it does say that in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And, of course, the people -- the person that you mention as having stopped the situation was either those persons mentioned in the paragraph there at line 6. There's two names mentioned there, because I don't want to identify the names, in view of the protective measures.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you agree with me you don't mention Rasula there either.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: It is correct. I didn't mention him.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I note the time, and I can indicate I've dealt with that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just have a -- have you any idea how much more time you would need, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in view of the tendency the witness has to sometimes not answer the question that you're asking and to go into other detail, I couldn't confirm a precise time at this point, but I'm certain we'll finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the next break will be a bit longer because for all kind of technical issues, like redactions and other matters. So we'll resume at 1.00, and if you could finish by today.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, before I give you the opportunity to resume your cross-examination, I have to correct in a technical way some of the language I used this morning. When I said "partially granted your motion," of course the motion was denied, but what I had in mind was that the schedule then indicated was a schedule which, I'm fully aware, not as you wished, but at least to some extent meets some of the concerns of the Defence. But just in order to avoid confusion, the motion was denied, but there was -- yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. And I'm grateful for the correction to the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Oh, yes, and I have -- the Judges would have a few questions for the witness, unless you put them to the witness. So if there would remain another 10 to 15 minutes for us, that would be fine; we could then excuse this witness. So let's try to proceed as efficiently as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that, Your Honour. Of course, as I indicated previously, the timing is not entirely in my hands, but we'll just see where we go from here.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I just want to take you to paragraph -- the paragraphs from 11 to 13 of your statement. If you could just turn to those paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you indicate in paragraph 13 -- you name a number of names in paragraph 13. Are you uncomfortable about being asked about one of those names in public session, and would you prefer to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That is, yes, you would prefer to go into private session or yes, you're happy to stay in public session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes. Because those names have already been mentioned in my earlier testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I do think that they have no specific relation with this witness, so therefore please -- we can proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Your Honour, I just noticed -- noted the reaction of the witness during the evidence in chief, and I'm very anxious to ensure that this aspect does not recur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, the names mentioned there --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I apologise for stepping up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And maybe I'm misunderstanding, but I understood the witness to indicate that he would prefer to go into private session for the reason given, not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he said these names were mentioned already, previously, so I thought -- but let's just check. Witness, could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. These names were mentioned in my earlier testimonies, so if they are mentioned, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you then do not mind if we continue in open session, especially since, as far as I understand, you know these names, you know who these people are, but they have no direct link, no personal link with you at special events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They don't have any direct connection with me, except for some other names that were already mentioned earlier in my earlier testimonies, so it is easy to link things up, to put two and two together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I -- Ms. Loukas, I think we could continue in open session, but as soon as we reach a point where a specific event is the subject of the testimony which could link this witness to other persons which are, I would say, of -- I take it that these people are notoriously known in the Sanski Most area by anyone, so therefore we could continue in open session. But I will keep a close eye on it, and if you would do the same. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm about to mention a name straight away, Your Honour. That's why I mentioned the matter, for abundant caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you'll see in your paragraph 13 there, you state --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's about the middle of the paragraph. It's about the middle of the paragraph. You state that: "I know that he was part of the SOS because --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that's the only part which would -- yes, perhaps we'll turn into private session. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just to mention the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session again.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you to paragraph 9 of your statement. Do you have that before you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Do you have that before you, Witness? Yes. Now, you deal in paragraph 9 with this issue of checkpoints; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I take it that you're dealing with some specific examples in that paragraph and also generally the situation in Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to this question of checkpoints, I think you've indicated that after about April of 1992, that it was only the non-Serbs that were being controlled; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I said sometime after Bajram. That could be the end of March, beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And just in relation to that question, being fair, Witness, you are not in a position to say that all Serb cars were never searched, are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: What I could see when I was at the checkpoint: If a Serb vehicle was stopped and as soon as they saw it was Serb, they would let them go. Now, whether anyone carried out any controls when I wasn't there, I don't know. I'm only telling you about what I saw when I was at a checkpoint. I can't tell you what happened when I wasn't there. So if they stopped me and stopped a Serb -- they would stop people but they would open my boot and open the front of the car, where the engine is. They would look under the seats. However, if it was a Serb car, they would just look at the registration and driving licences and let them go, if that is what you're asking. It's not the same to check the documents and see who is the owner and say, "Drive on," or stopping me, "Open the boot. Open the front," take a mirror and look under the vehicle. That's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, of course you had no way of knowing which was a car containing a Serb person and a car containing a Muslim person in every case, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And, of course, being realistic, the entire municipality we're dealing with had about 60.000 people in total; correct? According to the 1991 census. You'd agree with that population aspect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Roughly so, round about that number. I don't know exactly, whether it was more or less, but round about that figure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you a question in relation to the Patriotic League, Witness. Now, were you aware that in 1991 the Patriotic League had 103 Municipal Staffs in about 106 municipalities in Bosnia? Were you aware of that? According to Sefer Halilovic's book.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I don't know that. That's one thing. Secondly, I never saw Sefer Halilovic, nor do I enjoy reading, but simply that doesn't interest me. I was not aware that there were so many. If there is any official document saying that, well, that is what it is, but I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel. Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I just want to take you to paragraph 6 of your statement. Do you have that in front of you, Witness? So you have paragraph 6 before you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you read a newspaper there. In fact, in paragraph 6 you indicate that: "Dr. Vukic was interviewed in an article in the paper Glas," and you indicate that certain statements are made there; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you indicate that you've specially read this article and that you believe it was October of 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, of course, Witness, you're absolutely certain you've read this article, or else you wouldn't have put it in your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And that you read this article in Glas.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes, the name of the newspaper was Glas, and it was from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to that, you say that you believe it was October of 1991. I take it that you're saying this could go back as far as September and perhaps as far forward as November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I believe that it was in October, because it was at that time that I took my child to the hospital in Banja Luka, and that's when I bought a newspaper at the bus stop in Banja Luka, to have something to read. However, it is possible that it was -- but I remember that I took my child to the hospital in Banja Luka and I bought the newspaper at the bus stop in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you're satisfied that we're talking about October; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, is it possible that you're mistaken about this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Loukas, are we talking still about the date? Because you say, "You're satisfied that we're talking about October; correct?" "Yes." And then you say, "It's possible that you're mistaken about this." Is that still the date or about the content of the article or the doctor who gave the interview?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, it's more appropriate to rephrase it, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So I'm putting -- I'm asking you -- I'm suggesting that the situation is that you've possibly made a mistake about reading in the newspaper Glas the particular statements you've made there, that you say Dr. Vukic made in October of 1991 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I don't believe that I made a mistake, in view of the fact that I took my child to Banja Luka to Paprikovac, to the hospital there.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Is it possible that you're perhaps exaggerating what was contained in this newspaper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I quoted from the paper. And if the author of the article had exaggerated in what he wrote, then it's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, I'm suggesting that -- well, let me put it to you this way, Witness 565: Our investigators have researched the articles in Glas newspaper for September, October and November, and it appears that no such article exists. Now, in the light of that, are you prepared to concede that it's possible that you're mistaken about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: No. There could not have been a mistake, because I was not the only one having read that. There was my daughter there with me. She was 14 at the time. A neighbour of mine was sitting next to me, and we all wondered whether it was Dr. Vukic from the village next to mine and whether it was possible for him to have said something like that. I know him. I know where his house is. I know where he was born.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So, Witness, you're not prepared to concede the possibility of a mistake; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 565
utterances.text: I don't know how to concede to that. I read it in the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Any need to further question -- to put further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd very briefly like to make two points in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And if we could remain in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not in private session. We are no open session. We can return to private session. You always can check just by pushing the button of the video monitor, because you'll find "PS" in the top-right corner when we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session again. Mr. 565, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague and to have answers questions not only of the parties but also of the Bench. I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honour. Thank you for having the patience to hear me through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of July, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.07 p.m.,
